title: The Road of Life opens

facts.text: Since September 1941 German and Finnish forces had cut Leningrad off by land. Frozen Lake Ladoga became the city's only link to the rest of the Soviet Union.
From 20 November 1941 the bread ration fell to its lowest level of the siege: 250 grams a day for workers and 125 grams, about three thin slices, for everyone else.

On 22 November 1941 a column of 60 trucks led by Major V. A. Porchunov set out across the ice. It was the first motor convoy on the ice road, known as Military Road No. 101 and later as the Road of Life.
Most of the trucks were GAZ AA "polutorkas", light trucks rated at a ton and a half. By the most common account, the first run brought back 33 tons of flour.
The ice was still thin and the trucks often broke through. Many drivers stood on the running board and steered with the door open, so they could jump clear if the truck went down.
In the first week about 40 trucks fell through the ice, and the toll tripled the week after.
The stakes were the city itself. Deaths from hunger and cold climbed to about 100,000 a month in January and February 1942.
On 25 December 1941, as supplies began to arrive over the ice, the ration was raised for the first time: 350 grams for workers and 200 grams for others.
From November 1941 to April 1942 the ice road carried more than 350,000 tons of cargo into Leningrad, most of it food.
On the way back the trucks carried people out. Between 22 January and 15 April 1942 alone, 554,186 civilians were evacuated across the lake.
The ice road was declared out of service on 21 April 1942. It was rebuilt the next winter and ran again until 30 March 1943.

Photo by Yevgeny Khaldei, from russiainphoto.ru via Wikimedia Commons, tagged PD Russia and PD Russia 1996 (public domain in the U.S. per the file page). Saved 960 x 645 (Commons thumbnail; the Commons original is only 1024 x 688). Not dated to 22 November. Caution: the two fighters look sharper than the rest of the print and may be a darkroom addition, common in Soviet press photos; if Brian prefers, frame below them (they sit in the top third) or use the runner up. Runner up: a frame from the noon film, The Battle of Russia reel 8 at about 05:03, a truck convoy coming toward the camera across the snow (1440 x 1080 after pillarbox crop). declassified.fact: The engineers had worked out that a truck carrying one ton needed at least 20 cm, about 8 inches, of ice under it. When patrols measured the lake on 17 November 1941, they found only about 10 cm.

film.record: The Battle of Russia (1943, U.S. War Department, Why We Fight 5), 111-OF-5 reel 8 (NARA 36071)
film.shot_notes: Whole reel 8 of 10, 10 min 17 s (Part 2 of the film starts at reel 6, so the Film Library's Part 2 00:22:28 to 00:24:50 falls at about reel 8 04:04 to 06:26). Narration and score throughout, so the clip runs silent. Times are reel times, accurate to a second or two. 04:00 to 04:26 animated map of Lake Ladoga with swastikas (avoid). Ice road: 04:28 to 04:34 empty lake ice; 04:36 to 04:50 tractors and men breaking a track across the ice; 04:52 to 04:58 a road grader clearing snow; about 05:00 a traffic controller by a sign reading Lake Ladoga; 05:01 to 05:06 a column of trucks coming toward the camera across the snow; 05:06 a fuel tanker; 05:08 to 05:10 flour sacks piled in a truck; 05:12 to 05:16 the track running across the lake. NOON: open on the truck convoy at about 05:01 and run through the flour sacks to about 05:16, or open on the tractors at 04:36. Further usable: 05:18 to 05:50 German bombers overhead, an antiaircraft gun firing on the ice, trucks driving through bomb bursts; 05:52 to 06:00 a night convoy with headlights. Leave out 06:02 onward (the 1943 railway, a train marked To the heroes of Leningrad, evacuees at a station, then troops in snowsuits attacking). Enough distinct footage for a second cut if ever needed (tractors and grader 04:36 to 04:58 versus the air attack 05:18 to 05:50), but none is planned. Soviet film inside a U.S. film; not German film.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. War Department, Why We Fight series); the footage inside it is Soviet newsreel used in a U.S. government film (the Videos doc's route to the Eastern Front). NARA use status 'Restricted, Possibly', the routine flag on this series.
film.date_note: Soviet film of the Ladoga ice road from the winter of 1941 to 1942, shown in the U.S. Army's The Battle of Russia (1943). The shots are not dated to 22 November 1941, so the caption should say Soviet film of the ice road, winter 1941 to 1942.

video.note: Soviet film of the Lake Ladoga ice road, winter 1941 to 1942, inside The Battle of Russia (1943, U.S. War Department, Why We Fight 5), 111-OF-5 reel 8 (NARA 36071). The U.S. film carries narration and score, so the clip runs silent. Cut 19 Nov 2026 from footage/1941-11-22-ladoga-reel.mp4 (pillarbox cropped): 5:00.9 to 5:04.9 a column of trucks coming toward the camera across the snow; 4:36.0 to 4:41.0 tractors breaking a track across the ice; 4:48.6 to 4:51.6 a road grader clearing snow; 4:59.35 to 5:00.65 the traffic controller by the Lake Ladoga sign; 5:08.8 to 5:11.8 flour sacks piled in a truck. The map (4:00) and the 1943 railway (6:02 on) are left out. Shots are not dated to 22 November 1941.

body:
Major V. A. Porchunov led 60 trucks onto ice that was still too thin to trust. Behind him was a city where the bread ration for everyone but workers had fallen to 125 grams a day.

22 November 1941. Leningrad had been cut off by land since September. Its one link to the rest of the Soviet Union was Lake Ladoga, now frozen. Porchunov's column set out across it that day, the first motor convoy on what was called Military Road No. 101. People came to know it as the Road of Life.

Most of his trucks were GAZ AA polutorkas, light trucks rated at a ton and a half. By the most common account, the first run came back with 33 tons of flour.

The ice kept giving way. Many drivers rode standing on the running board, steering with the door hanging open so they could jump if the truck broke through. About 40 trucks went under in the first week.

It was worth the risk. Hunger and cold were killing about 100,000 people a month by early 1942. On 25 December, with food coming across the lake, the ration went up for the first time. By April the ice road had carried more than 350,000 tons into the city, and on the way back it carried out more than half a million civilians.
